title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: You are given an elevation map `height` as a list of non-negative integers. Each index is a bar of width 1. Compute how many units of water can be trapped between the bars after raining. Return a single integer.
starter_code:
def trap(nums):
    # Two pointers from the ends; track left_max and right_max
    left, right = 0, len(nums) - 1 if nums else -1
    return 0

predict_steps.prompt: With left at 0 and right at the last index, left_max starts as 0 and right_max as 1. Which pointer advances first when height[left] <= height[right]?
predict_steps.hint: Move the side with the smaller height.

predict_steps.prompt: At index 2 (value 0) between taller neighbors, how many units are trapped in that cell alone in the classic demo?
predict_steps.hint: min of bounding maxes minus height.

viva.question: What is the time and extra-space cost of trapping rain with two pointers?
expected_points: one linear pass over the elevation map is enough
extra memory stays constant beyond a few scalars
each index is charged water at most once
left_max and right_max update in constant time per step

viva.question: What breaks on a strictly increasing height array?
expected_points: no right wall is ever shorter than the water level on the left
left_max grows with every step so nothing is enclosed yet
water needs a lower bar bounded by taller walls on both sides

viva.question: Why does water at index i equal the lower bounding max minus height[i]?
expected_points: the water surface is limited by the smaller of the two side maxima
the bar itself displaces height[i] units of that column
the column cannot rise above the opposite bound either
the two-pointer rule always fills from the side whose max is currently smaller
